🎯This Lesson’s Objectives▼ Expand
❓
Big Question
Today’s Wonder

Four knights hang on a gallery wall, and some of the plaques under them are not true. How can you tell which moments you can trust?

🎯
Objectives
By the end of this lesson…
⚖️Contrast: I will name where two knights differ, and see why each difference is a place to argue from.
📖Back to the book: I will reread the pages for my two knights and learn four words for judging a knight.
🖼️Audit: I will check twenty plaques against the book and judge each one real and fair, twisted, or not in the book.
🛡️Evidence: I will hang an early, a middle and a late moment under each of my two knights, write my claim, and check my outline.
📝Writing: I will think about my evidence in writing.

contrast verb
To set two things side by side and see where they differ.
📌 Compare
To see how two knights are alike.
📌 Contrast
To see where they differ. The differences matter most.
📌 Every real difference
is a place where your argument can stand.
Gawain keeps every promise but one. Gareth serves a whole year without a word of complaint. Two different kinds of good.

2
✏️ Daily Oral Language
Study the model, then fix the sentence.
✅ Correct model
Mara packs her bag, and then she says, “I am ready.”

The word I and the names of people start with a capital letter: Mara, I. Two complete sentences cannot be joined by a comma alone: split them with a period, or join them with a comma and a joining word such as and. A speaker’s exact words go inside quotation marks, after a comma, with the end mark inside the closing mark.

🔧 Fix this one
Step 1 Tap the words that need a capital letter. 0 / 2
Step 2 Two sentences are run together after lace. Choose a fix.
Step 3 Choose the way to write Gawain’s words so a reader can hear him speak.

🪶 Poetry Corner

Tennyson’s poem tells of a lady who weaves in a tower and sees the world only in a mirror. Here is how she sees Sir Launcelot ride by. You will read more of it over the next three lessons.

Alfred, Lord Tennyson (1809–1892)
0:45
AI voice reading, not a recording of Tennyson. Photograph: Julia Margaret Cameron, 1865, public domain (source).
🖋️ Pen: Tennyson shows Launcelot as a knight of dazzling outward show. Tap every word that proves it.
The Lady of Shalott
Alfred, Lord Tennyson (1842 text), Part III
Tennyson spells his name Lancelot; our book says Launcelot.
A bow-shot from her bower-eaves, He rode between the barley sheaves, The sun came dazzling thro’ the leaves, And flamed upon the brazen greaves Of bold Sir Lancelot. A redcross knight for ever kneel’d To a lady in his shield, That sparkled on the yellow field, Beside remote Shalott. [Omitted: two stanzas] His broad clear brow in sunlight glow’d; On burnish’d hooves his war-horse trode; From underneath his helmet flow’d His coal-black curls as on he rode, As he rode down to Camelot. From the bank and from the river He flashed into the crystal mirror, “Tirra lirra,” by the river Sang Sir Lancelot.
bower-eaves: the edge of the roof over her room · greaves: armour for the shins · brazen: made of brass · redcross knight: a knight with a red cross on his shield · remote: far away · burnish’d: polished bright · trode: stepped · “Tirra lirra”: a carefree singing sound
Does all that shine prove he is a good knight?

When Gareth first comes to King Arthur’s court, what does he ask for?
Your answer
Professor Lovelore

Your answer
Professor Lovelore
Why does Launcelot refuse to try the sword in the floating stone?
Your answer
Professor Lovelore

Three knights, three different kinds of good. Gareth asks for almost nothing. Gawain fails once, out of fear. Launcelot says he is not worthy. Setting them side by side to see where they differ is called contrast. The differences are where your argument will stand.

🖼️ The Knight’s Gallery
Four knights, twenty plaques: check each one against your book

Professor Lovelore How this works

1Judge each plaque against your book.

3Hang an early, a middle and a late moment under each.
4Write your claim.
5Check last week’s outline and fix what is missing.
The Long Gallery
Step 1 Tap a plaque, check it against your book, then judge it. Real and fair: it happened, and the plaque keeps its meaning. Twisted: it happened, but the plaque bends what it means. Not in the book: it never happened.
Step 2 Choose two knights. Tap the star on a portrait.
Step 3 Hang the evidence. Under each knight, hang an early, a middle and a late moment, in the order the book tells them. Only plaques you judged real and fair can hang, or a moment from your own chart.
Choose two knights to open this step.
Step 4 The claim card. In one sentence, which of your two knights better fits Green’s idea of a good knight, and why?
Hang all six moments, each with its phrase, to open this step.
Step 5 Outline check. Your outline from last week is checked against five lines. Fix any line that is not lit.
Write your claim to open this step.
  • All 20 plaques judged
  • Two knights chosen
  • Three moments under each, in book order, each with a phrase
  • Claim written
  • Outline check: all five lights on
Portraits: AI-generated illustrations in the style of a medieval manuscript portrait (Codex Manesse). The gallery is drawn for this lesson.
